result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.eulerian_circuit()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find an Eulerian circuit in the graph if one exists. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L24726-L24800){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.eulerian_circuit() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Eulerian circuit](/assets/graphs/eulerian-circuit.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two triangles sharing node C, so every node has even degree. The Eulerian circuit starts and ends at C and uses each of the six edges exactly once; edges are numbered in the order the circuit takes them, and the card lists C, E, D, C, A, B, C." width="100%"} An Eulerian circuit is a closed trail that visits every edge exactly once, starting and ending at the same node. Uses Hierholzer's algorithm. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Optional[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs forming the Eulerian circuit, or `None` if no circuit exists. The circuit starts and ends at the same node. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} An Eulerian circuit traverses every edge exactly once and returns to its starting node, and Hierholzer's algorithm (1873) constructs one in $O(E)$ time by repeatedly stitching sub-circuits together as soon as they close. The construction only works if one actually exists: every node must have even degree in the undirected case, or in-degree equal to out-degree in the directed case, and the graph must be connected on the vertices that carry edges (weak connectedness suffices in the directed setting). Call `is_eulerian()` first if that's not guaranteed, since this method simply returns `None` when the preconditions fail. Semi-Eulerian graphs (open Eulerian trail, no circuit) need a slightly different variant that starts at one of the two odd-degree nodes. The circuit returned here is one of possibly many valid ones. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a cycle graph, the circuit visits every node and returns to the start, so its length is always one more than the number of edges: ::: {#3430480d .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(5) circuit = graph.eulerian_circuit() # Returns 6 (5 edges, plus the return to the start) len(circuit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 6 ``` ::: ::: A path graph has no Eulerian circuit (only endpoints have odd degree, so there's no way to return to the start), and the method reflects that by returning `None`: ::: {#42ba95e8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(5) circuit = graph.eulerian_circuit() # Returns None (path has no circuit) circuit ``` ::: The same holds for directed graphs, as long as every node's in-degree equals its out-degree: ::: {#1797e35a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=True) graph.add_cycle_graph(5) circuit = graph.eulerian_circuit() # Returns 6 (visits 5 edges, then returns to the start) len(circuit) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 6 ``` ::: :::
